newsitem.title: USA: Capacity use still a good price guide-SF Fed study.
newsitem.headline: Capacity use still a good price guide-SF Fed study.

text.p: The Federal Reserve Board's measure of industrial capacity utilization remains a valuable predictor of inflation, despite changes in the economy, an economist at the San Francisco Federal Reserve Bank said.

"Although there have been some structural changes in the U.S. economy, the basic indicator value of capacity utilization has endured," Joe Mattey, senior economist at the San Francisco Fed, wrote in the latest issue of the bank's "Economic Letter."
The Fed board publishes monthly indexes on industrial capacity utilization for a variety of sectors.
The latest data showed the overall industrial capacity utilization rate at 83.3 percent in September, above the 82 percent post-World War II mean.
The October rate is scheduled to be released Friday at 9:15 a.m. EST (1415 GMT), along with figures on industrial output.
U.S. economists in a Reuter survey predict a capacity utilization rate of 83 percent for October with no change in industrial output.
Some economists have linked increases in inflation with capacity utilization rates above 82 percent.
Mattey pointed out that although 82 percent is an imprecise estimate for an inflationary danger zone, a range of 78.5 percent to 83.5 percent would be more accurate.
In his article, Mattey argued that capacity utilization has been a relatively stable inflation indicator over a long period during which structural economic changes have occurred.

"This finding runs counter to some observers who suggest that 'globalization,' the shift of employment to the services sector and rapid technological change should have altered the relationship substantially," he said.

The San Francisco Fed economist stressed that it is important to examine the correlation with inflation by factoring in short-run food and energy price shocks and the role of long-term monetary policy influences.
Looking at the relationship with the so-called "core" Consumer Price Index, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, can be useful, Mattey said.
He also emphasized that capacity use is more strongly correlated to the acceleration of inflation than to its level.
Looking at data between 1967 and 1996, Mattey concluded, "capacity utilization has a relatively strong correlation with the acceleration of core consumer price inflation."
Additionally, he said that capacity use has tended to track trends in the jobless rate, suggesting its ability to reflect the broad state of the economy.
The so-called "natural" jobless rate or non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU) has also been widely used as a tool for predicting inflation.
However, Mattey said that given variations in the NAIRU over time, capacity utilization has an advantage over NAIRU as a "simple" indicator of inflation trends.

As for the argument that increased international trade has rendered domestic capacity utlization less useful, Mattey noted that imports still make up a relatively small portion of the total amount of goods purchased in most sectors.

He also said that despite the shift to services, factory operating rates are still good predictors of inflation, given the extent that they can provide indications of overall demand and their correlation with cyclical activity in labor markets.
